rows.description: A preschooler learns that hugging or kissing is a choice, with a right to say no, even to relatives. Adults who accept a wave or high-five instead teach the child that their body belongs to them.

A teenager learns to ask or check before hugging a friend and to accept no gracefully. Stating a preference, such as I am not a hugger, is healthy; pressure or guilt over refusal is a warning sign to discuss with a trusted adult.

A young adult uses a firm no, a raised palm or a step away to set a boundary, or a light push to get free from unwanted touch. Others must stop at once; if ignored, leaving and seeking help or reporting is appropriate.

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A child repeats that a group is greedy or lazy, echoing what was heard at home. The child has no evidence, only borrowed words; a calm question such as how do you know helps.

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A child laughs at jokes about a region, faith or accent because friends do. Laughing feels like belonging, though the joke may hurt someone present; a friend who does not laugh shows another way.

rows.subtopic: Stereotypes and how to challenge them
rows.description: A young adult realises they assumed a stranger would behave a certain way based on dress or name, and felt uneasy. Noticing a bias honestly, without self-punishment, is how it begins to weaken.
A child who told a fib to avoid trouble soon believes the version they told; repeating a story makes it feel like memory.
A teenager who skims the notes feels sure they know the material and is shocked by the result; the feeling of familiarity is mistaken for understanding.
A student tells themselves they want the family-approved career while feeling dread each morning; the mind edits inconvenient wishes to keep the peace.
A young child remembers the one time he was scolded more strongly than the many times he was praised. Painful moments feel heavier and stick longer.
A teenager replays one mocking comment for days and shrugs off warm praise from friends. The mind is tuned to threat, which can distort self-worth.
A young adult keeps checking bad news and negative posts and concludes the world is worse than it is. Distress rises while real information does not.
A teenager sees a video or voice note of a famous person or classmate saying something shocking and believes it. Synthetic media can look and sound real, so the medium itself is no longer proof.

rows.subtype: Deepfake used to shame or extort [Receiver]
rows.description: A young person finds fake images or videos of themselves circulating, or is threatened with them for money. It is not their fault, and saving evidence, reporting to the platform and cyber police, and telling a trusted adult are the right steps.

A teenager preparing for an interview or public speaking practises standing straight and taking a breath, which can help nerves. Confidence also comes from preparation; exaggerated power poses do not replace real skill.

A young worker hunches over a laptop for hours, which reads as focus or exhaustion to others and can cause discomfort. Regular movement, an adjusted chair and breaks help body and mood, and coworkers should not assume laziness from posture.
